strengths: Soundness: The core memory contribution has credible empirical support. With the same backbone and training data, Table 1 reports improvements over similarity merging on Video-MME Long, LVBench, VideoEvalPro, and ELViM even without the memory reader. This makes the gains more persuasive than comparisons against independently trained systems.

Significance: Memory-constrained, query-independent processing of long videos is a useful problem. Figures 6–7 show advantages across memory budgets and input lengths, supporting the practical value beyond a single operating point.

Originality: Adapting fast-weight TTT to streaming video understanding, with a delayed reconstruction objective, is a useful extension of existing TTT methods. Table 2 compares against both standard TTT and Mamba-2; Table 10 further examines the prediction span.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript is generally well organized and supplies mathematical objectives, architecture details, training datasets, hardware costs, and substantial ablations. It states that implementation code and ELViM questions accompany the supplementary material, although those artifacts were not available for this review.

Benchmark and ethics: ELViM provides 1,849 questions spanning 15 categories, with human checking and explicit attempts to reduce prior-knowledge shortcuts. The impact statement appropriately discusses privacy, persistent harmful information, consent, and memory deletion.
weaknesses: ELViM supports delayed episodic recall more directly than procedural learning or skill reuse. The identical target video is replayed before asking what happens next; no transfer to a new demonstration, setting, or task execution is tested. Moreover, Table 6 evaluates the same models used to filter questions, so their near-chance partial-video and near-perfect full-video performance is largely built into selection. A history-removal control for the proposed model and evaluation on held-out filtering models would strengthen the benchmark's validity.

The memory-reader contribution is incompletely isolated. Section 5.1 doubles stored memory when reading is enabled, so the gains combine larger retained context with a different reading algorithm. Similar GPU footprints make this a useful system comparison, but do not establish that modality-aware selection itself causes the improvement. The AdaReTaKe comparison needs explicit matching of stored tokens, chunk size, retained KV budget, and non-multimodal token handling.

Some implementation details leave the fixed-memory claim difficult to reproduce precisely. Section 3.3 introduces an average budget M but selects m entries in Equation 8, while preserving other tokens without an explicit cap. The treatment of accumulated timestamps/text and the buffer needed for delayed TTT targets should be specified. Table 7 also lacks a workload denominator for its FLOP figures, limiting interpretation of the claimed negligible overhead.

The incremental mechanisms have limited uncertainty analysis. Stage 2 improves several results by only 0.3 percentage points, and the long-span objective generally adds roughly 1–2 points over standard TTT. No repeated-run variation or paired confidence intervals are supplied. Figure 8 lacks bin counts and uncertainty, and its curves nearly coincide in several distance ranges; it therefore provides suggestive rather than conclusive evidence about improved distant-memory retention.

Quantitative reporting needs reconciliation: similarity merging scores 38.5 on ELViM in Table 1 but 35.4 in Table 2 under apparently comparable settings. The abstract's approximately 15-point ELViM improvement is 14.2 points against the stronger reported non-streaming baseline, and the claim of consistent 3–7-point long-video improvements overstates the 1.7-point Video-MME Long gain. These issues do not erase the broader positive results, but weaken precision.

Limitations and dataset governance could be more explicit. The paper should distinguish visual fast-weight memory from audio memory, since audio bypasses TTTMEM, and acknowledge that same-video recall does not establish procedural transfer. Collection licenses, redistribution arrangements, and human annotation procedures for ELViM are not adequately described. Upload dates after mid-2025 alone also do not establish the claimed guarantee of exclusion from both proprietary models' training data.

strengths: Soundness: The controlled comparisons provide credible evidence that the proposed memory improves long-video QA. Using the same backbone and training data, Table 1 reports gains over similarity merging on LVBench (55.6 versus 51.6), VideoEvalPro (58.9 versus 51.8), and ELViM (46.7 versus 38.5). Improvements remain without the memory reader, supporting the contribution of TTTMEM itself.

Originality: Adapting fast-weight test-time training to streaming video understanding is a useful contribution. The backward-prediction objective provides a concrete extension beyond standard TTT; Table 2 and Appendix G support its incremental benefit. Comparisons with Mamba-2 and standard TTT help distinguish this contribution from simply adding recurrence.

Significance: Understanding hours of video with bounded working memory is practically important. The memory-budget and frame-count sweeps show useful behavior beyond a single operating point. ELViM also contributes a substantial delayed-recall evaluation, with 1,849 questions across 1,021 target videos and 15 categories.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture and training stages are generally understandable, and the manuscript supplies major architectural settings, training resources, benchmark statistics, and multiple ablations. It states that code and benchmark questions accompany the supplementary material, although those artifacts were not available for this review.

Ethics: The impact statement appropriately identifies privacy, persistent storage of harmful or biased information, and computational costs. The manuscript presents no evident material ethical obstacle to acceptance. Overall, the demonstrated memory improvements justify weak acceptance, despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: Claim validity: ELViM replays the same target video and asks about its upcoming content. This establishes delayed episodic recall more directly than acquisition and transfer of procedural knowledge. There is no evaluation on a different demonstration, altered task instance, or actual task execution. Claims about continual learning and reusable procedural skills therefore exceed the evidence.

Benchmark validity: Questions are selected using failures on partial videos and successes on full videos from Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen3-VL. Consequently, Table 6 largely reflects the selection procedure rather than independently validating shortcut resistance. An independent evaluator and a matched removal or replacement of the earlier target-video occurrence would better establish dependence on episodic memory. Uploading videos after mid-2025 also does not, by itself, guarantee their absence from the models' training data.

Reporting consistency: Similarity merging scores 38.5 on ELViM in Table 1 but 35.4 in Table 2, without an explained configuration difference. This changes the apparent ablation gains. The abstract's '15%' improvement is 14.2 percentage points against the stronger non-streaming ELViM baseline, while the claimed consistent 3–7-point long-video gains do not describe Video-MME Long, where the improvement is 1.7 points.

Statistical support: No repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, or paired significance analyses are provided. This particularly limits conclusions about stage-two training, whose gains are only 0–0.3 points in Table 2, and the smaller long-span prediction gains. Figure 8 also needs sample counts per temporal-distance bin to substantiate the retention analysis.

Method specification: Section 3.3 introduces a target cache size M but selects k=m in Equation 8, leaving the relationship between chunk size and retained memory unclear. The handling and budgeting of retained non-multimodal tokens, initial chunks without a lagged target, and fast-weight initialization/reset should be explicit. Table 7 additionally lacks a clear input workload and FLOP-counting convention.

Scope and limitations: The strongest comparisons cover two reimplemented streaming memory algorithms rather than the broader range of retrieval-based streaming systems discussed in related work. This supports improvement over the tested baselines but limits the broad state-of-the-art claim. A focused limitations discussion should distinguish bounded-memory recall from procedural transfer and describe the uncertainty associated with the synthetic concatenation-and-replay benchmark.

strengths: Soundness: The core memory contribution has credible empirical support. Under the matched backbone and training-data setup, TTTMEM without reading improves over similarity merging on LVBench (55.4 versus 51.6), VideoEvalPro (55.8 versus 51.8), and ELViM (43.9 versus 38.5). These improvements do not depend on the additional reading mechanism.

Originality: Adapting fast-weight TTT to streaming video memory is a useful contribution. The historical reconstruction objective adds a concrete extension, supported by comparisons against standard TTT and Mamba-2, prediction-span ablations, and analyses across memory sizes and input lengths.

Significance: Understanding hours-long video under bounded working memory is practically important. ELViM contributes 1,849 questions across 1,021 target videos and 15 categories, with timestamp filtering and human checking. It provides a useful test of delayed episodic recall.

Presentation and reproducibility: The architecture, objectives, and training stages are generally clearly explained. Training datasets, hardware, learning rate, frame limits, and several architectural hyperparameters are reported; the manuscript also states that code and benchmark questions accompany the supplement. Runtime and larger-memory experiments strengthen the practical evaluation.

Research ethics: The impact statement appropriately recognizes privacy, persistent storage of harmful information, and computational costs, and discusses consent and memory-reset mechanisms. The manuscript presents no evident material ethical barrier to acceptance.
weaknesses: ELViM supports delayed recall more directly than procedural learning or transfer. The query replays the same target video, rather than testing application to a new demonstration or situation. Its average duration is approximately 49 minutes and maximum approximately 92 minutes (Table 4), so descriptions of learning from videos observed 'hours earlier' overstate this benchmark. An ablation removing the initial target presentation for the proposed model would better establish dependence on stored experience.

Benchmark filtering introduces evaluation-selection effects: questions are retained based on failures and successes of Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen3-VL, so their near-chance partial-video and near-perfect full-video results are partly consequences of construction. Upload dates and this filtering also do not establish the Appendix A claim that the videos are guaranteed absent from those models' training sets.

Several numerical claims need correction. Similarity merging obtains 38.5 on ELViM in Table 1 but 35.4 in Table 2 without an explained configuration change. The reported 8.8-point improvement over PEMF is 8.5 points from Table 1. Improvements are also less uniformly large than the abstract suggests: Video-MME long improves by 1.7 points over video-SALMONN 2+, and VideoEvalPro improves by 4.0 points over the strongest listed offline result.

Evidence for individual additions is weaker than evidence for the overall system. Stage 2 contributes only 0–0.3 points in Table 2, and long-span prediction contributes roughly 0.9–1.6 points over standard TTT. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are provided. Figure 8 also lacks sample counts and uncertainty by temporal-distance bin, limiting conclusions about retention at particular distances.

Memory accounting and implementation details need clarification. The reading configuration doubles stored tokens while matching approximate GPU usage, so the main reading ablation changes both capacity and retrieval; Appendix F only partly resolves this. Section 3.3 introduces an M-token budget but selects m tokens while retaining non-multimodal tokens, without fully specifying their bound. Buffering historical targets, fast-weight initialization/reset, and the handling of early chunks also deserve explicit documentation.
